screens.title: Handling Events and Real-time Updates in dApps
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on events: the lightweight on-chain signals that let your dApp react immediately when a smart contract state changes. You will learn what an event is, why emitting an event is different from reading contract state, and how to subscribe to those signals from a browser using Ethers. js. We’ll use a Greeter contract example that emits a GreetingUpdated event, then connect that contract to a React component which listens, updates UI state, and cleans up listeners to avoid memory leaks. Along the way you’ll learn to filter events efficiently using the indexed keyword and to balance real-time updates with network stability and performance. By the end of the chapter you will be able to update a deployed contract, add a listener in the frontend, and confirm the UI refreshes immediately after a transaction is mined. Think about how this changes the user experience: instead of polling every few seconds, your interface gets notified as changes land on chain. A quick question to keep in mind: what UI element in your dApp should respond first when an event arrives, and why?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Handling Events
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Events power real-time dApps

You will learn how Solidity emits events and how the browser can subscribe to them. This reduces polling, improves responsiveness, and helps you build more interactive user experiences.

In this lesson
Define events, emit them in Solidity, and wire listeners with Ethers.js.
Coming up
Filter events by indexed params and prevent memory leaks with proper cleanup.
Hands-on
Update Greeter.sol, deploy, then add a useEffect listener in React to show live updates.
Why it matters
Events let your dApp react instantly to state changes with minimal network overhead.
Explore Key Topics
Events
On-chain logs emitted by contracts; efficient notifications for dApps.
Listeners
Use Ethers.js to subscribe and react in real time, updating state and UI.
Filters
Index parameters let nodes pre-filter events, saving bandwidth and CPU.
Live example: Greeter
GreetingUpdated event drives immediate UI refresh
Emit an event from setGreeting, then listen using greeterContract.on to update the page when a new greeting appears.
Quick note
Always remove listeners when components unmount to prevent memory leaks and duplicate handlers.

Third, you will design UI updates that respond to incoming events without over-fetching contract state. screens.title: What are Smart Contract Events?
screens.narratorSegment: A smart contract event is a structured log entry emitted during a transaction that is stored in the transaction receipt and indexed by nodes. Unlike persistent contract storage, events are optimized for historical records and external consumption. When a contract emits an event, that data becomes part of the block's logs and can be retrieved cheaply compared to writing additional storage or repeatedly calling view functions. A concrete example is a Greeter contract that emits GreetingUpdated with the updater address, old greeting, new greeting, and a timestamp whenever setGreeting runs. Your frontend can subscribe to that event so the UI updates immediately when the transaction finalizes. A common misconception is treating events like an authoritative source of current state; they represent a historical record of changes but should be reconciled with contract reads when you need the authoritative current value. To summarize, events give you a time-ordered stream of relevant changes; they are ideal for notifications, activity feeds, and driving UI updates while contract reads remain the single source of truth for current state. What are Smart Contract Events? means events are blockchain log entries emitted by contracts and stored in the transaction receipt for external subscribers.. In practical terms, events as on-chain logs for external listeners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event Definition
keyIdea.text: Events are blockchain log entries emitted by contracts and stored in the transaction receipt for external subscribers.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › What are Events?
Definition
Events are on-chain logs

When emitted, events are recorded in the transaction receipt and can be subscribed to by off-chain apps. They are efficient for history and notifications, not for storing authoritative current state.

How it helps
  • Provide immediate notifications to a dApp after a transaction completes.
  • Reduce the need for frequent polling of contract state.
  • Offer a historical timeline useful for activity feeds and audits.
Key Takeaway

Use events for timely notifications and history; read contract state for the authoritative current value.

Concrete example
A Greeter emits GreetingUpdated(updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting, timestamp). Off-chain listeners receive the four values and can display who changed the greeting and when.
Misconception
Events are not authoritative current state. They record state changes; verify current state by calling view functions when necessary.
Check your understanding
If an event shows a new greeting but a contract read still returns the old greeting, what should you trust and why?

screens.title: How Events Appear on Chain
screens.narratorSegment: Events are produced during transaction execution and become part of the transaction's logs when the transaction is mined. The flow is: contract code calls emit with parameters; the EVM appends a log entry to the transaction receipt; the miner includes the receipt in the block; nodes index log topics and make them queryable. For clients, an event arrives either via subscription from a node or by fetching historical logs; subscription delivers near-instant notifications as blocks land. A concrete example: when setGreeting calls emit GreetingUpdated, the transaction receipt contains the four values and an indexed topic for any indexed parameters. A misconception is expecting events to be delivered exactly once in all environments — network reconnections or node-specific indexing can cause duplicates or missed messages. To handle this, design listeners that tolerate duplicate events and reconcile with a read of contract state when necessary. In short, know the lifecycle: emit → receipt → block inclusion → node indexing → client delivery; each step has implications for latency, filtering, and reliability. How Events Appear on Chain means emit creates a log in the transaction receipt; nodes index logs and make them available to subscribers and historical queries.. In practical terms, from emit to transaction receipt and client delivery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Emit creates a log in the transaction receipt; nodes index logs and make them available to subscribers and historical queries.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Event Lifecycle
Numbered Flow
1. emit in contract
Contract execution triggers the event and adds a log entry to the transaction context.
2. included in receipt
The receipt contains the event data once the transaction is mined.
3. node indexing
Nodes index topics for efficient filtering and retrieval.
4. client delivery
Subscribed clients receive events or fetch historical logs as needed.
Reality check
Expect possible duplicates or missed events under network interruptions; design reconciliation into your listener logic.
Concrete example
When setGreeting emits GreetingUpdated, the receipt holds updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting, and timestamp. A subscribed frontend receives those values and can update the greeting display immediately after the receipt is indexed.
Best practice
Treat events as signals to refresh or reconcile specific pieces of UI rather than a trigger to re-fetch your entire application state indiscriminately.

screens.title: Defining and Emitting Events in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: In Solidity you declare an event with a name and parameter types, then call emit inside a function when state changes. The chapter example defines event GreetingUpdated(address indexed updater, string oldGreeting, string newGreeting, uint timestamp). The indexed keyword marks parameters that nodes index as topics so they can be filtered efficiently. A concrete pattern is to index addresses or small numeric identifiers that you will later filter by. After updating greeting in setGreeting, emit the event with the old and new values and block timestamp. A common mistake is indexing every parameter — only indexed parameters become topics and there is a limit on how many topics are convenient. Another gotcha is assuming non-indexed fields can be filtered at the node level; they cannot. They must be inspected client-side after fetching logs. Practically, keep the event small, index only what you need to filter on, and use events as signals; call a contract read when you need the current canonical value. Defining and Emitting Events in Solidity means declare events with parameter types; use emit to record a log and indexed for node-level filtering.. In practical terms, use event declarations, emit, and indexed parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: Here we examine the concrete Greeter contract changes used in the chapter. The contract declares GreetingUpdated and emits it inside setGreeting with the updater address, old and new strings, and timestamp. This gives the frontend both who changed the value and the new text to display. When you deploy this updated contract, remember to update the ABI used by your frontend so the event signature and parameter ordering match what the client expects. A typical pitfall is deploying an updated contract but leaving an old ABI in the frontend, which prevents the client from decoding logs or attaching listeners correctly. keyIdea.text: Update the contract, redeploy, and refresh your frontend ABI so listeners can decode and subscribe to events properly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Greeter.sol
Contract snippet
// contracts/Greeter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Greeter {
  string public name;
  string private greeting;

  event GreetingUpdated(address indexed updater, string oldGreeting, string newGreeting, uint timestamp);

  constructor(string memory _name, string memory _greeting) {
    name = _name;
    greeting = _greeting;
  }

  function greet() public view returns (string memory) {
    return string(abi.encodePacked(greeting, ", ", name, "!"));
  }

  function setGreeting(string memory _newGreeting) public {
    string memory _oldGreeting = greeting;
    greeting = _newGreeting;
    emit GreetingUpdated(msg.sender, _oldGreeting, _newGreeting, block.timestamp);
  }
}
After deployment, verify the transaction receipt includes the GreetingUpdated log and update your frontend ABI so the event signature decodes correctly.

screens.title: Subscribing with Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Ethers. js exposes a simple A P I for subscribing to contract events. Using a Contract instance, call contract. on('EventName', listener) to receive event arguments and an event object when the event fires. The listener receives parameters in the same order as declared in Solidity, followed by a final event metadata object. In a React app, set up this subscription inside a useEffect that depends on the contract instance. The cleanup function should call contract. off('EventName', listener) to remove the handler when the component unmounts or the instance changes. A concrete example in the chapter shows a listener that sets latestEvent in state and calls fetchContractData to reconcile UI state. A common error is adding a listener each render without removing prior listeners, causing duplicated handlers and memory leaks. Also be careful about binding context or creating anonymous functions inside useEffect without stable references; that can prevent off from matching the listener to remove it. Always use a named function or stable callback so greeterContract. off removes exactly the handler you added. Subscribing with Ethers.js means use contract.on to subscribe and contract.off in useeffect cleanup to safely manage listeners in single-page apps.. In practical terms, greetercontract.on() and cleanup with greetercontract.off(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Ethers.js Subscription
JS Listener
// Listener signature example
const listener = (updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting, timestamp, event) => {
  setLatestEvent({ updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting, timestamp: new Date(Number(timestamp) * 1000).toLocaleString() });
  fetchContractData(greeterContract);
};

greeterContract.on('GreetingUpdated', listener);
// Later: greeterContract.off('GreetingUpdated', listener);
Listener arguments arrive in Solidity-declared order followed by an event object. Use a stable reference so off can remove it.
React lifecycle
Set up the listener inside useEffect when the contract instance is available, and return a cleanup function that removes the listener to avoid leaks.
Tip
Prefer named functions or useRef to hold the handler so you can reliably remove it in cleanup.

screens.title: useEffect Pattern for Event Listeners
screens.narratorSegment: A robust React pattern places event subscription within useEffect so the listener exists only while the component needs it. The effect depends on the greeterContract instance; when the contract becomes available, create a named listener, call greeterContract. on('GreetingUpdated', listener), and return a cleanup that calls greeterContract. off('GreetingUpdated', listener). This pattern prevents duplicate listeners if the component re-renders and avoids attempts to update state after unmount. A concrete example from the chapter shows logging to the console when the event arrives, updating latestEvent state, and calling fetchContractData to reconcile displayed values. Common mistakes include defining the listener inline without stable references, which makes off unable to find and remove the handler, and relying on window-level subscriptions that persist across navigation. Also avoid heavy synchronous work in the listener; update state and schedule necessary fetches but keep the listener lightweight. Finally, if you must re-create the handler based on new props, remove the old handler first and add the new one in the same effect so you never have overlapping listeners. useEffect Pattern for Event Listeners means add listeners in useeffect and remove them in cleanup; use stable references to prevent duplicate or dangling handlers.. In practical terms, set up once, clean up reliably, and avoid duplicate handlers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › useEffect Pattern
Pattern
useEffect(() => {
  if (!greeterContract) return;
  const listener = (updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting, timestamp, event) => {
    setLatestEvent({ updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting, timestamp: new Date(Number(timestamp) * 1000).toLocaleString() });
    fetchContractData(greeterContract);
  };

  greeterContract.on('GreetingUpdated', listener);

  return () => greeterContract.off('GreetingUpdated', listener);
}, [greeterContract]);
This creates the listener only when greeterContract changes and removes it on unmount or change.
Pitfalls
  • Anonymous handlers inside useEffect prevent reliable removal.
  • Adding listeners on every render causes duplicate callbacks.
  • Heavy synchronous work in listener increases UI lag; keep it light.
Pro tip
If you re-create the listener for new props, remove the previous one first in the same effect to avoid overlap.

screens.title: UI Update Strategies: Re-fetch vs Targeted Update
screens.narratorSegment: When an event arrives, you must decide whether to re-fetch all contract state or update only specific UI elements. Re-fetching everything ensures correctness but can cause extra latency and node work. Targeted updates use the event payload to change only what matters immediately, which is faster and more efficient. For example, GreetingUpdated includes the newGreeting value; your frontend can directly set the greeting message from the event and optionally confirm by a targeted read of greet() later. A common misunderstanding is assuming every event should trigger a full refresh — for complex dApps this leads to over-fetching and poor performance. Instead, adopt a hybrid approach: apply the event payload immediately to improve perceived responsiveness and schedule a lightweight reconciliation to verify canonical state if needed. This approach balances user experience with correctness. Also consider potential race conditions when multiple events or transactions arrive in short order; queue or timestamp updates to apply them in the correct order and avoid UI flashes caused by late-arriving receipts. Indexed example

event GreetingUpdated(address indexed updater, string oldGreeting, string newGreeting, uint timestamp);
Index the address you will filter by, such as updater, to enable node-side filtering.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Performance Notes
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter highlights several common mistakes developers make when adding event listeners. First, forgetting to remove listeners causes memory leaks and duplicate callbacks. Always call contract. off in the useEffect cleanup. Second, over-fetching state after every event causes unnecessary load; prefer targeted updates and scheduled reconciliations. Third, assuming perfect delivery from nodes is risky—connections can drop, resulting in missed events. Use server-side indexing services or re-query historical logs on reconnection when reliability is critical. Another issue is misusing indexed: only indexed fields are server-filterable. If you need to filter by a large string, consider emitting an identifier you can index instead. Finally, listener implementations must be lightweight; heavy synchronous processing can block the main thread and harm UI responsiveness. The practical takeaway is to design listeners to be resilient, efficient, and minimal: remove them when not needed, rely on indexed filters where possible, and plan for reconciling state after network interruptions. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on events: the lightweight on-chain signals that let your dApp react immediately when a smart contract state changes. You will learn what an event is, why emitting an event is different from reading contract state, and how to subscribe to those signals from a browser using Ethers. js. We’ll use a Greeter contract example that emits a GreetingUpdated event, then connect that contract to a React component which listens, updates UI state, and cleans up listeners to avoid memory leaks. Along the way you’ll learn to filter events efficiently using the indexed keyword and to balance real-time updates with network stability and performance. By the end of the chapter you will be able to update a deployed contract, add a listener in the frontend, and confirm the UI refreshes immediately after a transaction is mined. Think about how this changes the user experience: instead of polling every few seconds, your interface gets notified as changes land on chain. A quick question to keep in mind: what UI element in your dApp should respond first when an event arrives, and why?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain and use smart contract events to power real-time frontends. First, you will define what events are and why they are stored in transaction receipts rather than contract storage. Second, you will implement event listeners in a frontend using Ethers. js and React, including correct lifecycle setup and cleanup. Third, you will design UI updates that respond to incoming events without over-fetching contract state. Finally, you will use indexed parameters and contract filters to efficiently subscribe only to the events your dApp cares about. Each objective links a practical skill to a user-facing outcome: responsive interfaces, reliable subscriptions, and efficient network use. A concrete example is updating a Greeter contract to emit GreetingUpdated and adding a useEffect hook which sets a latestEvent state and triggers a constrained refresh of the greeting message. Practice and verification milestones will ensure you can deploy the contract, wire the ABI into the frontend, and confirm real-time event-driven updates are visible in the UI and browser console.

This second objectives slide explains how you'll put the theory into practice. First, update Greeter. sol to emit GreetingUpdated when setGreeting runs and redeploy to a testnet or local node. Next, update your frontend ABI and add a latestEvent state value. Implement a useEffect hook that subscribes to GreetingUpdated, updates latestEvent, and calls a constrained fetch to refresh only the greeting display. Third, test the flow by changing the greeting in the UI, observing console logs for events, and verifying the interface updates without polling. Finally, apply filters by using greeterContract. filters. GreetingUpdated(specificAddress) to subscribe only to events from a particular updater. Each practice step has a verification: event logged in the console, latestEvent rendered in the UI, and no duplicate listeners after navigation. This practice-centered objective ensures you can deploy, wire up listeners, and confirm a responsive, efficient dApp.

A smart contract event is a structured log entry emitted during a transaction that is stored in the transaction receipt and indexed by nodes. Unlike persistent contract storage, events are optimized for historical records and external consumption. When a contract emits an event, that data becomes part of the block's logs and can be retrieved cheaply compared to writing additional storage or repeatedly calling view functions. A concrete example is a Greeter contract that emits GreetingUpdated with the updater address, old greeting, new greeting, and a timestamp whenever setGreeting runs. Your frontend can subscribe to that event so the UI updates immediately when the transaction finalizes. A common misconception is treating events like an authoritative source of current state; they represent a historical record of changes but should be reconciled with contract reads when you need the authoritative current value. To summarize, events give you a time-ordered stream of relevant changes; they are ideal for notifications, activity feeds, and driving UI updates while contract reads remain the single source of truth for current state. What are Smart Contract Events? means events are blockchain log entries emitted by contracts and stored in the transaction receipt for external subscribers.. In practical terms, events as on-chain logs for external listeners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Events are produced during transaction execution and become part of the transaction's logs when the transaction is mined. The flow is: contract code calls emit with parameters; the EVM appends a log entry to the transaction receipt; the miner includes the receipt in the block; nodes index log topics and make them queryable. For clients, an event arrives either via subscription from a node or by fetching historical logs; subscription delivers near-instant notifications as blocks land. A concrete example: when setGreeting calls emit GreetingUpdated, the transaction receipt contains the four values and an indexed topic for any indexed parameters. A misconception is expecting events to be delivered exactly once in all environments — network reconnections or node-specific indexing can cause duplicates or missed messages. To handle this, design listeners that tolerate duplicate events and reconcile with a read of contract state when necessary. In short, know the lifecycle: emit → receipt → block inclusion → node indexing → client delivery; each step has implications for latency, filtering, and reliability. How Events Appear on Chain means emit creates a log in the transaction receipt; nodes index logs and make them available to subscribers and historical queries.. In practical terms, from emit to transaction receipt and client delivery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In Solidity you declare an event with a name and parameter types, then call emit inside a function when state changes. The chapter example defines event GreetingUpdated(address indexed updater, string oldGreeting, string newGreeting, uint timestamp). The indexed keyword marks parameters that nodes index as topics so they can be filtered efficiently. A concrete pattern is to index addresses or small numeric identifiers that you will later filter by. After updating greeting in setGreeting, emit the event with the old and new values and block timestamp. A common mistake is indexing every parameter — only indexed parameters become topics and there is a limit on how many topics are convenient. Another gotcha is assuming non-indexed fields can be filtered at the node level; they cannot. They must be inspected client-side after fetching logs. Practically, keep the event small, index only what you need to filter on, and use events as signals; call a contract read when you need the current canonical value. Defining and Emitting Events in Solidity means declare events with parameter types; use emit to record a log and indexed for node-level filtering.. In practical terms, use event declarations, emit, and indexed parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Here we examine the concrete Greeter contract changes used in the chapter. The contract declares GreetingUpdated and emits it inside setGreeting with the updater address, old and new strings, and timestamp. This gives the frontend both who changed the value and the new text to display. When you deploy this updated contract, remember to update the ABI used by your frontend so the event signature and parameter ordering match what the client expects. A typical pitfall is deploying an updated contract but leaving an old ABI in the frontend, which prevents the client from decoding logs or attaching listeners correctly.
